background.definition: A posterior hip dislocation is marked by the head of the femur lying posterior to the acetabulum, with a typical attitude of shortening, internal rotation, and adduction of the involved lower extremity. In an anterior hip dislocation, the femoral head lies anterior to the acetabulum, with a typical attitude of abduction and external rotation of the lower extremity.

list.listitem: Incidence of hip dislocation is 0.1 per 10,000 civilian residential population, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Hospital Discharge Summary from 1998 to 2001.
Traumatic dislocation of the hip accounts for 2% to 5% of all joint dislocations.
Most are posterior hip dislocations. Anterior dislocations are less common and account for 3% to 9% of all hip dislocations.
One percent of hip dislocations occur bilaterally.

The majority of patients with a dislocated hip have been involved in high-energy trauma (i.e., motor vehicle accident). However, dislocation may result from sports trauma or falls, especially in the elderly or those with connective tissue disorders.

Instability is one of the most common complications of total hip arthroplasty, with the first three months after surgery being the most high risk time for prosthetic hip dislocation. A recent study showed that 2.3% of a large cohort of primary total hip replacement patients experienced dislocation within 2 years.

In patients who have undergone total hip arthroplasty, direct anterior approach (HR 0.27) and a lateral approach (HR 0.58) were associated with a lower risk of dislocation compared with the posterior approach. Following revision, use of a dual mobility construct (HR 0.40) and acetabular revision were associated with a lower risk of dislocation.
Posterior dislocation frequently results from a dashboard injury in which the flexed hip is pushed posteriorly by an impact of the knee on the car dashboard.
Anterior dislocations may be caused by levering the hip out by forcible external rotation of the abducted hip or by forced extension of the straight limb.
Seat belt use can help prevent hip dislocations. In one series, only 4 of 38 patients with a hip dislocation were restrained, whereas the other 34 were unrestrained (P < .05). B
Dashboard design, handling, braking, and other safety features can minimize the likelihood of injury in motor vehicle crashes. C

Hip fracture/dislocation may result from simple falls, especially in the elderly. Interventions that can help reduce falls in the elderly include muscle strengthening, balance retraining, Tai Chi, and home hazard assessment. B
Hip bandages do not prevent subsequent dislocation in patients with history previous total hip arthroplasty dislocation.
If the patient presents with multiple trauma, attend to airway, breathing, and circulation as the first priority. C
If the patient complains of hip pain or presents with significant trauma, obtain plain AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs of the pelvis. C
If hip dislocation is identified, this is an orthopedic emergency. Obtain emergent orthopedic consultation or consider urgent reduction if orthopedic consultation is not available. B

list.listitem:
One commonly used classification system for posterior dislocations of the hip is listed below:
Type I: Dislocation with or without minor fracture. Type II: Dislocation with a large single fracture of the posterior acetabular rim. Type III: Dislocation with comminution of the posterior acetabular rim with or without a major fragment. Type IV: Dislocation with fracture of the acetabular floor. Type V: Dislocation with fracture of the femoral head.
Typically, there is a history of trauma, characteristically, with a high-energy mechanism of injury.
The patient may have multiple injuries, but if conscious, will generally complain of hip, pelvis, and/or thigh pain.
In a posterior dislocation, the affected leg is classically shortened, adducted, flexed, and internally rotated.
In an anterior dislocation, the affected leg is classically abducted and externally rotated.
Assess neurovascular status when dislocation is known or suspected.

A plain AP radiograph of the pelvis is a standard screening tool after major trauma and will be diagnostic of hip dislocation in the majority of patients. Lateral and oblique radiographs increase sensitivity and aid in further characterizing the deformity. Lateral or oblique Judet views are essential in evaluating associated acetabular fractures.
CT scanning may add additional information, but is rarely necessary for initial diagnosis.
Emergent orthopedic consultation is indicated, and your orthopedic consultant can help guide imaging decisions.

After reduction, plain radiographs are indicated to confirm reduction and rule out associated femoral head and acetabular wall fractures. In addition, CT scanning is indicated postreduction to assess the adequacy of reduction and detect chondral and osteochondral fragments retained in the joint. If clinical suspicion warrants, MRI is superior in defining chondral loose bodies or other soft-tissue defects.
Begin evaluation in multiple trauma patients with airway, breathing, and circulation.

If fracture or dislocation is suspected order AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs of the pelvis. If clinical suspicion is high, Judet views are indicated to evaluate for associated acetabular fractures.
If hip dislocation is identified, this is an orthopedic emergency. Obtain emergent orthopedic consultation or consider urgent reduction if orthopedic consultation is not available.

Hip dislocations should be reduced as soon as possible to reduce the likelihood of complications such as femoral head osteonecrosis or sciatic nerve injury (i.e., within 6 hours, according to some authors). B

Different techniques have been advocated for closed reduction of a hip dislocation. Generally, this entails adequate sedation/analgesia followed by slow, steady longitudinal traction along the femoral axis accompanied by maneuvers to relocate the joint (e.g., Allis and Stimson maneuvers). C
Postreduction rehabilitation should be prescribed by the orthopedic surgical consultant.

Classically, it was taught that hip dislocations should be reduced within 12 to 24 hours to reduce the likelihood of complications. However, based on more recent data, this recommendation has been shortened to within 6 hours.

Different techniques have been advocated for closed reduction of a hip dislocation, all of which require longitudinal traction along the femoral axis accompanied by maneuvers to relocate the joint. Slow, steady, traction with adequate sedation/analgesia will improve the likelihood of success. Two of the earliest described and most commonly used maneuvers, Allis and Stimson, are described below.

Allis maneuver: the patient is supine. An assistant stabilizes the pelvis. Axial traction is applied with the patient's hip and knee flexed at 90°. Lastly, the hip is internally and externally rotated to help achieve reduction.

Stimson maneuver: the patient is prone. The affected leg is allowed to hang over the edge of the stretcher. An assistant stabilizes the pelvis. With the hip and knee flexed to 90°, downward traction is applied to achieve reduction.

A type I dislocation is treated by closed reduction, if possible, followed by immobilization (e.g., in Buck traction). Consensus has not been reached as to when to begin mobilization, but evidence suggests that early ambulation does not lead to worse outcome. One author recommends resuming weight bearing when pain and spasm disappear.
There is a paucity of evidence from RCTs comparing operative and nonoperative treatments for recurrent dislocation following total hip replacement.

In a series of 3326 consecutive patients who underwent hemiarthroplasty for a fracture of the neck of the femur, 46 experienced a subsequent discloation. Most (70%) occurred within one month of surgery, and all but one within 3 months. Most required surgery to reduce the dislocation.

In a case series of 151 patients at higher risk of dislocation (high BMI, age 75+, alcohol use) use of a dual mobility bearing in a primary total hip arthroplasty resulted in only 1 dislocation during a 3.6 year follow-up.
Orthopedic referral is indicated in most every case of hip fracture/dislocation. However, prompt reduction is vital, without assistance from an orthopedist if necessary.

Complications, including heterotopic ossification, avascular necrosis, and nerve injury (e.g., sciatic), appear to be directly related to the length of time before reduction of the dislocation. For instance, in a report of 127 hip dislocations, osteonecrosis occurred in 4% of hips reduced within 6 hours and in 58% of hips that remained dislocated for more than 6 hours.
If avascular necrosis is suspected, MRI is most sensitive for diagnosis. Management options can include surgery (e.g., total hip arthroplasty) and conservative management.
The best treatment is prevention, by reducing the dislocation as soon as possible.
In a review of 128 dislocations and fracture-dislocations, there were no good results in hips that remained dislocated longer than 24 hours. B

In a review of 127 posterior hip dislocations, 88% of those that were reduced within 6 hours after dislocation had an excellent or good result (i.e., no appreciable pain or limp, except after a long hard day of work, no avascular necrosis, and no more than 25% restriction in range of movement). B

In a systematic review of 17 articles (13,722 patients) on the impact of obesity on total hip arthroplasty (THA), obesity (BMI >30) was associated with younger age at the time of THA and a four-fold higher perioperative complication rate.
The diagnosis and management of child and adolescent traumatic hip dislocation is the same as in adults.

Developmental Dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in infants is commonly diagnosed within the first 3 months after birth. Late-presenting DDH (diagnosed after 3 months) occurs and is associated with cephalic presentation (vs. breech birth) and a swaddling history.
Most infants with a hip click but normal results on the Ortolani test and Barlow maneuver do not have hip dysplasia.

In a systematic review, rhe Barlow maneuver and the Ortolani maneuver had a sensitivity of 46%, a specificity of 99%, a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 52 (95% CI 21 - 127), and a negative likelihood ratio (LR-) of 0.55 (0.37 - 0.82) for identifying hip dislocation in infants. They are therefore useful when positive to rule-in the diagnosis, but do not rule it out when negative or normal.
